foods.name: Water Leaf
foods.explanation: Rich in iron and antioxidants. Reduces inflammation and supports hormonal balance.

foods.name: Bitter Leaf
foods.explanation: Anti-inflammatory properties. May help regulate blood sugar levels — beneficial for PMOS.

foods.name: Njama-Njama (Huckleberry)
foods.explanation: High in calcium and folate. Supports overall health and reduces oxidative stress.

foods.name: Garden Eggs
foods.explanation: Low calorie, high fibre. Supports gut health and blood sugar control.

foods.name: Okra
foods.explanation: High soluble fibre slows glucose absorption. Excellent for blood sugar management.

foods.name: Eru (African Jointfir)
foods.explanation: Protein-rich leafy vegetable. Supports hormone production and muscle health.

foods.name: Okok / Afang
foods.explanation: Rich in minerals and protein. Reduces insulin resistance when eaten regularly.

foods.name: Unripe Plantain
foods.explanation: Low glycaemic index. Releases energy slowly, helping to stabilise blood sugar for PMOS.

foods.name: Local Red Rice
foods.explanation: Higher fibre and lower GI than white rice. Better blood sugar control for PMOS.

foods.name: Oat-Based Fufu
foods.explanation: High beta-glucan fibre. Reduces blood sugar spikes and improves cholesterol.

foods.name: Plantain Fufu
foods.explanation: Made from unripe plantain, this fufu has a lower GI than cassava fufu.

foods.name: Cocoyam
foods.explanation: Moderate starch content. Eat in smaller portions. Better than cassava for blood sugar.

foods.name: Irish Potato
foods.explanation: Moderate glycaemic load. Boiled is better than fried. Eat with proteins and vegetables.

foods.name: Cassava Fufu
foods.explanation: High GI starch. Causes rapid blood sugar spikes. Limit portions — try plantain fufu instead.

foods.name: White Rice
foods.explanation: High GI. Switch to red or brown rice for better blood sugar control with PMOS.

foods.name: Garri
foods.explanation: Very high GI when made into eba. Limit intake — causes rapid insulin spikes.

foods.name: Local Fish (Mackerel, Tilapia)
foods.explanation: Omega-3 fatty acids reduce inflammation and improve insulin sensitivity in PMOS.

foods.name: Smoked Fish (Canda)
foods.explanation: Good protein source. Rich in omega-3. Use in soups to add flavour and nutrition.

foods.name: Beans (Black-eyed, Red beans)
foods.explanation: High protein and fibre. Low GI — excellent for managing blood sugar in PMOS.

foods.name: Groundnuts (Peanuts)
foods.explanation: Healthy fats and protein. Moderate portions help reduce insulin resistance.

foods.name: Egusi (Melon Seeds)
foods.explanation: Rich in healthy fats, protein, and zinc. Zinc supports hormonal balance in PMOS.

foods.name: Crayfish
foods.explanation: High protein condiment. Rich in iodine which supports thyroid function.

foods.name: Bush Mango Seeds (Dika)
foods.explanation: Contains fibre that slows fat absorption. Used in Ogbono soup. Supports weight management.

foods.name: Chicken (lean, grilled)
foods.explanation: Lean protein without saturated fat. Grilled or boiled chicken is best for PMOS.

foods.name: Eggs
foods.explanation: Complete protein. Choline supports liver function which is important for hormone metabolism.

foods.name: Safou (African Pear)
foods.explanation: Rich in oleic acid (healthy fat) and antioxidants. Anti-inflammatory benefits for PMOS.

foods.name: Avocado
foods.explanation: Healthy monounsaturated fats. Reduces inflammation and supports hormone production.

foods.name: Guava
foods.explanation: High vitamin C and fibre. Low sugar content — safe for blood sugar management.

foods.name: Passion Fruit (Grenadelle)
foods.explanation: Low GI, high fibre. Supports digestion and steady blood sugar levels.

foods.name: Papaya (Pawpaw)
foods.explanation: Contains papain enzyme for digestion. Rich in antioxidants — eat in moderate portions.

foods.name: Orange
foods.explanation: Good vitamin C source. Eat whole fruit, not juice, to get the fibre benefit.

foods.name: Mango
foods.explanation: High in natural sugars. Limit to half a mango per serving. Rich in vitamins A and C.

foods.name: Pineapple
foods.explanation: Higher sugar content. Eat small portions. Good source of manganese and bromelain.

foods.name: Ripe Banana
foods.explanation: High natural sugars. Limit ripe bananas. Unripe plantain is a much better alternative.

foods.name: Red Palm Oil
foods.explanation: Rich in vitamin E and beta-carotene. Use in small amounts — high in saturated fat.

foods.name: Groundnut Oil
foods.explanation: Good for cooking at high temperatures. Use moderately — contains some saturated fat.

foods.name: Coconut Oil
foods.explanation: Contains medium-chain fatty acids. Use sparingly due to high saturated fat content.

foods.name: Mbanga Soup (Palm Nut Soup)
foods.explanation: Nutritious but high in palm oil. Eat with unripe plantain fufu instead of cassava fufu.

foods.name: Egusi Soup
foods.explanation: Rich in protein and healthy fats from melon seeds. Excellent when loaded with leafy greens.

foods.name: Eru Soup
foods.explanation: Very nutritious. High protein from eru leaves and waterleaf. Eat with unripe plantain.

foods.name: Ndolé
foods.explanation: National dish of Cameroon. Bitter leaf and groundnuts provide excellent nutrition for PMOS.

foods.name: Koki (Bean Cake)
foods.explanation: Steamed bean cake — high protein, low GI. An excellent PMOS-friendly snack or side dish.

foods.name: Achu Soup
foods.explanation: Nutritious but high in palm oil. Eat with cocoyam fufu in moderate portions.

foods.name: Soya Milk
foods.explanation: Plant-based protein and calcium. Supports bone health. Choose unsweetened versions.

foods.name: Zobo (Hibiscus Tea)
foods.explanation: Antioxidant-rich. May help lower blood pressure and reduce inflammation. Drink unsweetened.

foods.name: Ginger Tea
foods.explanation: Anti-inflammatory and may reduce menstrual pain. Drink regularly to ease PMOS symptoms.

foods.name: Soursop Leaf Tea
foods.explanation: Traditional anti-inflammatory tea. Supports immune function.

foods.name: Soft Drinks / Sweetened Juices
foods.explanation: Very high sugar content. Causes rapid insulin spikes. Replace with water, zobo, or ginger tea.

foods.name: Roasted Corn (Maize)
foods.explanation: Whole grain with fibre. Roasted corn has a lower GI than processed corn products.

foods.name: Roasted Groundnuts
foods.explanation: Healthy fats and protein. A handful between meals helps stabilise blood sugar.

foods.name: Garden Egg Salad
foods.explanation: Low calorie and high fibre. A great PMOS-friendly snack between meals.

foods.name: Biscuits / Crackers
foods.explanation: Refined flour and high sugar. Replace with roasted groundnuts or boiled beans.

foods.name: Chin Chin
foods.explanation: Deep-fried with high sugar. Causes insulin spikes. Eat very occasionally in small portions.

foods.name: Puff Puff
foods.explanation: Deep-fried high-GI snack. Replace with koki or roasted corn for better blood sugar control.

foods.name: Cow Skin (Kanda)
foods.explanation: High protein but also high in saturated fat. Eat occasionally in small portions.

foods.name: Bush Meat
foods.explanation: Lean protein source. Preparation method matters — grilled or boiled is better than fried.

foods.name: Fufu Corn
foods.explanation: Traditional staple. Moderate GI. Pair with vegetable soups to slow glucose absorption.

foods.name: Boiled Yam
foods.explanation: Moderate GI. Boiled yam is better than fried. Eat with proteins and vegetables.

foods.name: Borlotti / Kidney Beans
foods.explanation: Very high fibre and protein. Low GI — one of the best foods for PMOS blood sugar control.

foods.name: Lentils
foods.explanation: Excellent source of iron, protein, and folate. Low GI and anti-inflammatory.

foods.name: Moringa Leaves
foods.explanation: Extremely nutrient-dense. Rich in iron, calcium, and antioxidants. Supports hormonal balance.
